sentences.text: This dinosaur measured 15 meters in length and weighed 5 metric tons.
It stood 4 meters tall, representing a relatively small sauropod for its era.
Its skull featured an enigmatic second hole, a trait absent in Diplodocus and its close relatives.
The tail terminated in short, flat vertebrae that created a whip-like shape.
Excavated remains were in good condition, with skull bones preserved after partial exposure by erosion.
The name Suuwassea comes from the Crow language term for the first thunder heard in spring.
The specific name emilieae honors the late expedition sponsor Emilie deHellebranth.
Fossils were recovered during expeditions between 1999 and 2000 and formally described by Harris and Dodson in 2004.
A veterinary professor named William Donawick found a bone protruding from the ground while riding with his son-in-law.
Its discovery coincides with other medium-sized sauropod finds in the northern Morrison Formation, contrasting with large animal finds in the southern sectors.
In its original description, it was classified as Flagellicaudata incertae sedis due to a mix of primitive and derived traits found in both dicraeosaurids and diplodocids.
Later studies reclassified Suuwassea as a North American member of the family Dicraeosauridae, though it was previously placed in the subfamily Apatosaurinae.
It is more closely related to dicraeosaurids, sharing the second postparital foramen with Dicraeosaurus, Tornieria, and Amargasaurus.
Suuwassea lived during the Upper Jurassic in the Morrison Formation of southern Carbon County, Montana, USA.
It lived during the late Jurassic, approximately 147 million years ago in the Tithonian stage, in what is now North America.
The animal lived from the Kimmeridgian to the Tithonian stages, between 154.8 and 143.1 million years ago.
The presence of dicraeosaurid characters in a Laurasian diplodocoid raises open questions about the origin and distribution of ancestral diplodocooids.
Suuwassea raises the debate of whether the group Flagellicaudata originated in Laurasia or Gondwana.
It is debated whether dicraeosaurids existed before migrating from Laurasia, based on the primitive traits found in Suuwassea.
